vo.text: In 480 BC, the biggest army the ancient world had ever seen marched into Greece. And a few thousand Greeks decided to stop it. At a gap in the mountains.

The army belonged to Xerxes, King of Kings of Persia. His empire stretched from Egypt to India. Ancient writers said his army was millions strong. Modern historians think it was more like a hundred thousand or more. Still: a lot.
The Greek cities were usually busy fighting each other. This time, some of them teamed up.
They chose a narrow pass called Thermopylae. Steep mountains on one side. The sea on the other. A road so narrow that a giant army could only squeeze through a little at a time.
Holding it were about seven thousand Greeks, led by King Leonidas of Sparta and his three hundred Spartans.
Xerxes waited four days, expecting the Greeks to run away. They did not.
The historian Herodotus tells a story. Someone warned that the Persian arrows would be so many, they would block out the sun. A Spartan named Dienekes answered: Good. Then we will fight in the shade.
On the fifth day, the Persians attacked. Wave after wave poured into the pass. The Greeks held a wall of shields, and took turns at the front.
Even Xerxes' elite guard, the Immortals, could not break through. Herodotus says the king jumped up from his throne three times, afraid for his army.
Then a local man named Ephialtes sold a secret: a hidden mountain path that led around, behind the Greeks.
That night, the Immortals climbed the path.
Leonidas learned he was about to be surrounded. He sent most of the Greeks away. He stayed, with his Spartans and a few others who refused to leave, like seven hundred men from the town of Thespiae.
On the third day, surrounded on all sides, they fought to the very end.
So the Persians won. They marched south and burned Athens. Which sounds like the end of the story.
But those days bought the Greeks time. A few weeks later, the Greek navy smashed the Persian fleet at Salamis. And the next year, the Persians were beaten on land, for good.
Today, a stone at the pass carries an old message: Go tell the Spartans, passer by, that here, obeying their orders, we lie.
